summary: Describes how ISI implemented the Mail Transfer Protocol on TOPS-20 machines, supporting both sender and receiver roles over TCP and NCP. Mail is queued in files and a background program dispatches it.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 784 describes how ISI planned to implement the Mail Transfer Protocol on TOPS-20. A dispatcher reads queued mail, checks what each destination can accept, and sends it through a suitable channel.

subtitle: How ISI organized an MTP mail implementation for TOPS-20 systems.

tldr.problem: The TOPS-20 mail system needed a way to queue messages and send them through several available network and local delivery mechanisms.
tldr.mechanism: Mail is stored in a control file and a separate data file, then a dispatcher consults host capability tables and selects an output channel.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes the planned ISI TOPS-20 components for sending and receiving Mail Transfer Protocol traffic over TCP and NCP.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 784's status as Unknown. This RFC describes the ISI TOPS-20 implementation and its components.

sections.title: A Queue and Dispatcher for Mail
sections.content:
The memo describes an MTP implementation for TOPS-20 written in BLISS-10. Its planned sender and receiver functions support both TCP and NCP transport services and provide interfaces to other mail delivery mechanisms.

Mail programs create files in user directories. A background dispatcher sends queued mail, while a user-run dispatcher can send immediately when the needed channel is available.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail is placed in files and handled by a dispatcher. The dispatcher can run in the background or be started by a user.

sections.title: Separating Delivery Instructions from Mail
sections.content:
Each piece of mail uses two files. The control file contains delivery information and points to the second file, which contains the mail data, including the RFC 733 header.

This separation lets the dispatcher change the recipient information as it sends a message through different channels, while the message data stays available to read. If one channel is unavailable, the control file can retain information for recipients who have not yet been sent the message.
sections.plainLanguage: One file tells the system where to send the message. The other file holds the message itself, so delivery progress can change without rewriting its contents.

sections.title: Choosing an Output Channel
sections.content:
The dispatcher consults a host capability table to determine whether a destination accepts MTP over TCP, MTP over NCP, or the older FTP-over-NCP method. A separate table covers special cases, such as delivery through another mail system.

The system is made from receivers, senders, the dispatcher, mail composition programs, pending mail files, and local or external mail sources and destinations. The RFC says the first five network components were being built and describes the remaining interfaces and tables as work to provide or define.
sections.plainLanguage: The dispatcher checks a table to learn which delivery method each host supports. It then sends the message through that method or a special mail route.
